body:
Early warning and the role of IMD

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) monitors cyclonic disturbances over the North Indian Ocean using weather observations, satellites, radar, ocean information and forecasting models. Its warnings describe a developing system, its likely movement and intensity, and the expected adverse weather. They are updated as new observations become available.

IMD also supplies specialised warnings for coastal districts, ports and fishing interests. The warning must then be translated into local action through the state and district administration, maritime authorities, police, health services, local bodies and community organisations.

The 4-stage cyclone warning system

StageNormal advance periodMain purpose
Pre-cyclone watchAbout 72 hours before adverse weatherIndicates the likely development and potential coastal impact of a cyclone
Cyclone alertAt least 48 hours before adverse weatherDraws attention to threatened coastal areas and expected conditions
Cyclone warningAt least 24 hours before adverse weatherProvides more specific information for protective action
Post-landfall outlookAt least 12 hours before expected landfallIndicates likely weather effects as the system moves inland

The post-landfall outlook is normally issued before landfall, although it concerns conditions expected after landfall. The indicated times are standard advance-warning stages, not guaranteed intervals in every event. When a system forms near the coast or intensifies rapidly, warning stages may be shortened or issued directly.

From warning to evacuation

Evacuation means moving people away from an area where remaining would expose them to danger. District and local authorities identify threatened settlements using storm forecasts, coastal elevation, expected inundation and local vulnerability. They determine which areas should be evacuated and communicate instructions through appropriate channels.

Preparedness includes identifying safe routes and cyclone shelters, arranging transport where needed and communicating in a form residents can understand. Particular attention is necessary for older persons, children, persons with disabilities, pregnant women and people who cannot leave independently.

A cyclone shelter is a designated safe structure used to protect people from cyclone-related hazards. A suitable shelter needs more than a strong building: safe access, adequate space, drinking water, sanitation, basic health arrangements and arrangements for vulnerable residents are also important.

Coastal households should secure essential documents, medicines, drinking water, food and a battery-powered communication source where practical. Fishers should follow official marine warnings and avoid going to sea when dangerous conditions are forecast. Boats should be secured only when doing so remains safe; no one should expose themselves to dangerous winds or waves to protect property.

During and immediately after the cyclone

People in evacuated areas should remain in authorised shelters until the competent authorities permit return. They should not enter floodwater, approach broken power lines or seek shelter beneath unstable structures or trees. Weather conditions may remain dangerous after the centre of a cyclone has passed.

After the storm, authorities must establish whether roads, buildings, water supplies, electricity systems and health services are safe. Floodwater may contaminate drinking-water sources. Coastal flooding may also introduce saline water into agricultural fields and freshwater supplies.

Recovery includes restoring livelihoods

Immediate relief may provide shelter, food, water and medical assistance. Longer-term recovery includes repairing houses, restoring roads and electricity, supporting farmers and fishing households, and replacing or repairing damaged livelihood assets. A repaired fishing harbour is of limited benefit if fishing households cannot safely return to work or replace essential nets and equipment.

The experience of Cyclone Biparjoy illustrates the relevance of advance warnings. According to IMD's Annual Report 2023, the system crossed the Saurashtra–Kachchh and adjoining Pakistan coasts near Jakhau Port on 15 June 2023 as a very severe cyclonic storm. This is a historical event, not a current forecast.

Prelims focus

  • IMD provides cyclone forecasts and meteorological warnings.
  • The standard advance-warning sequence is 72, 48, 24 and 12 hours.
  • Post-landfall outlook concerns inland effects but is issued before expected landfall.
  • District authorities organise local protective action, including evacuation and shelter arrangements.
  • Cyclone Biparjoy crossed the coast near Jakhau, Kachchh, on 15 June 2023.
  • Trap: Meteorological warning and administrative evacuation order are different functions.

[Sources: IMD, Tropical Cyclone Operational Plan for the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, 2021, Annex II-C-6, Four Stage Warnings; IMD, Annual Report 2023, Cyclone Biparjoy case study, p. 122; GSDMA, State Cyclone Preparedness and Response Plan, preparedness, warning and response sections; GCERT Class 7, Social Science, Ch 13, Disaster Management; consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Cyclone Warning, Evacuation, Shelters and Recovery in Gujarat

body:
Drought is a slow-developing disaster

Drought develops when a prolonged deficiency of available water creates adverse effects on the environment, agriculture, water resources or society. Unlike a cyclone, it generally develops over weeks, months or longer. Its impacts may persist even after rainfall resumes because groundwater, reservoirs, agricultural production and household incomes can take time to recover.

Gujarat receives most of its annual rainfall during the southwest monsoon, but the amount and distribution vary widely. Kachchh, North Gujarat and parts of Saurashtra are particularly important regions for understanding recurrent drought and water stress. Much of South Gujarat is generally wetter, but individual locations there can still experience seasonal water shortages.

The 4 main types of drought

TypeMeaningTypical evidence
Meteorological droughtRainfall is substantially below the long-term normalRainfall deficiency over an area and season
Agricultural droughtSoil moisture is inadequate for cropsCrop stress, wilting or reduced yields
Hydrological droughtWater in rivers, reservoirs or groundwater becomes deficientLow reservoir storage, streamflow or groundwater levels
Socioeconomic droughtWater-related shortages disrupt livelihoods or essential needsLoss of income, fodder scarcity or drinking-water shortages

These categories describe different aspects of a developing problem. Rainfall deficiency may first reduce soil moisture, then affect streamflow or reservoir storage and eventually reduce agricultural production and livelihoods. The sequence is not fixed: an irrigated crop may initially withstand low rainfall, while a rainfed crop becomes stressed much earlier.

In IMD's published monsoon FAQ, meteorological drought is described using seasonal rainfall below 75% of the long-term average. This is a meteorological classification used in that reference. It is not, by itself, a universal rule for declaring government drought relief; official drought assessment can also consider crop conditions, water availability and other indicators.

Drought and water scarcity are not identical

Water scarcity means that available water is insufficient to meet requirements. It may arise from low rainfall, excessive extraction, high demand, poor distribution, contamination or inadequate storage. Therefore, a region can face water scarcity even without a meteorological drought.

Groundwater over-extraction is especially relevant where irrigation and settlement demand exceed natural replenishment. A good monsoon does not automatically restore an aquifer that has been depleted over many years.

Regional vulnerability in Gujarat

Dry and semi-arid conditions in Kachchh and parts of Saurashtra make rainfall variability important for crop production and livestock. North Gujarat also faces pressure on groundwater resources in areas where extraction is intensive. Rainfed farmers are vulnerable to delayed monsoon onset, long dry spells or rainfall occurring at unsuitable stages of crop growth.

For livestock-dependent households, drought can cause a combined shortage of drinking water and fodder. Falling agricultural output may reduce rural employment and purchasing power. Drought management must therefore address people, crops and animals rather than only measuring rainfall.

Preparedness and mitigation

Effective drought management combines supply protection with demand management.

  • Water conservation: repair leakage, reduce waste and encourage efficient household, farm and industrial use.
  • Rainwater harvesting: collect and store suitable rainfall runoff and support groundwater recharge where local conditions permit.
  • Efficient irrigation: use appropriate methods such as drip irrigation to reduce unnecessary water loss.
  • Crop planning: select crops and sowing practices suited to local rainfall and available irrigation, supported by weather advisories.
  • Drinking-water protection: plan reliable supplies for vulnerable settlements and protect essential domestic needs.
  • Livelihood support: arrange appropriate fodder, employment and other assistance when drought affects households and livestock.

Water harvesting and irrigation efficiency are useful but not complete solutions. Their effectiveness depends on rainfall, groundwater conditions, crop choices, maintenance and the total quantity of water withdrawn.

Prelims focus

  • Meteorological drought concerns rainfall deficiency; agricultural drought concerns soil moisture and crops.
  • Hydrological drought concerns rivers, reservoirs and groundwater.
  • Socioeconomic drought concerns shortages affecting people and livelihoods.
  • Kachchh, North Gujarat and parts of Saurashtra are important Gujarat water-stress regions.
  • The IMD monsoon FAQ uses seasonal rainfall below 75% of the long-term average to describe meteorological drought.
  • Trap: Water scarcity can result from excessive demand or groundwater extraction even when rainfall is not unusually low.

[Sources: India Meteorological Department, Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon, section on definitions and types of drought, consulted 2 November 2026; GSDMA, State Disaster Management Plan 2023–24, Vol. I, Ch 3, Drought Hazard Profile; GCERT Class 7, Social Science, Ch 13, Disaster Management; GCERT Class 11, Geography, Ch 14, Disaster Management.]

body:
How flooding occurs

A flood occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. Flooding may be caused by excessive rainfall, rising river levels, rapid runoff, obstruction of drainage, storm surge or a combination of these factors.

Flood risk depends not only on how much rain falls at a particular location but also on rainfall in the upstream catchment, river capacity, local drainage, terrain, land use and the condition of water-control infrastructure.

Distinguishing major flood types

Flood typePrincipal processTypical exposed area
River floodRiver water rises beyond its banks or spreads across the floodplainLow-lying land near a river
Flash floodWater levels rise rapidly after intense runoff or another sudden releaseSmall catchments, channels and downstream settlements
Urban floodRainwater accumulates because runoff exceeds effective drainage capacityRoads, built-up neighbourhoods and underpasses
Coastal inundationElevated sea water enters low-lying coastal landCoastal settlements, estuaries and port areas

These categories can overlap. A city may experience both river flooding and urban waterlogging during the same storm. Near a coast, elevated sea levels can also make it more difficult for rainwater or river water to drain into the sea.

Important Gujarat examples

The Tapi River and Surat illustrate the significance of river conditions, upstream rainfall and urban exposure. The Narmada River and Bharuch illustrate the importance of downstream river levels and estuarine conditions. The Sabarmati and Ahmedabad are relevant to riverfront and urban flood planning, while the Vishwamitri and Vadodara illustrate the challenges of river flooding within a densely populated city.

These examples identify a river-city relationship; they do not imply that every historical flood in those cities had a single cause. Urban drainage failure, local heavy rainfall, river conditions and land-use changes may contribute differently to individual events.

Why urbanisation can increase flood damage

Natural soil and vegetation allow some rainfall to infiltrate and slow the movement of runoff. Roads, roofs and other hard surfaces generally reduce infiltration and move water more rapidly towards drains and low-lying areas. When natural channels or wetlands are filled, narrowed or obstructed, the available space for water decreases.

Encroachment on floodplains increases the number of people and buildings directly exposed to river flooding. Blocked stormwater drains can cause serious waterlogging even where a river has not overflowed.

Forecasting and preparedness

IMD issues weather and heavy-rainfall forecasts. The Central Water Commission (CWC) provides river flood forecasting services at designated locations. Local administrations use such information together with reservoir conditions, local observations and vulnerability assessments to issue public instructions.

Risk reduction includes keeping drains functional, protecting natural drainage paths, monitoring river levels, avoiding unsafe occupation of floodplains and maintaining suitable temporary shelters. Wetlands, permeable surfaces and rainwater-retention areas can help reduce rapid runoff, although they cannot eliminate severe flooding.

Public precautions and recovery

  • Follow local flood warnings and move to designated safe areas when instructed.
  • Do not walk, swim or drive through flowing floodwater; its depth, current and hidden obstacles may be difficult to judge.
  • Keep away from damaged electric lines, submerged electrical equipment and unstable structures.
  • Do not consume water or food suspected of contamination by floodwater.
  • Return to affected buildings only when safe access and essential conditions have been established.

After a flood, safe drinking water, sanitation, waste removal, disease surveillance and the inspection of damaged buildings and services are major recovery concerns. Electrical repairs and other hazardous restoration work belong to authorised personnel.

Prelims focus

  • Tapi is an important river for understanding Surat's flood exposure.
  • Narmada is an important river for understanding Bharuch's downstream flood exposure.
  • Vishwamitri is associated with Vadodara; Sabarmati with Ahmedabad.
  • IMD forecasts rainfall, while CWC has a specialised role in river flood forecasting.
  • Urban flooding can occur without a major river overflowing.
  • Trap: Heavy rain at a city is not the only possible cause of flooding there; upstream rainfall and river conditions can also matter.

[Sources: GCERT Class 7, Social Science, Ch 13, Disaster Management; GCERT Class 9, Social Science, Ch 20, Disaster Management; GSDMA, State Disaster Management Plan 2023–24, Vol. I, Ch 3, Flood Hazard Profile; India Meteorological Department, Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon, section on floods; Central Water Commission, Flood Forecasting Services, consulted 2 November 2026.]
